question: What is this object (stirrup, shape, ceramic vessel)?
answer:
This object is considered a Moche Stirrup Spout vessel. It is assigned this distinction because of its unique spout that has two tubes connecting to one opening or spout. Stirrup pots are unlike many other Moche vessels. Many water vessels in the Moche culture were made to be stagnant, unmoving from their intentional storage space. The unique part of the Stirrup vessel is the stirrup spout itself. The spout doubles as a handle that is in a perfectly human design. The spout fits in the human hand well and allows for easy transportation. Stirrup vessels also tend to be smaller in size which make them far more easy to transport, rather than long-term and larger water storage vessels. 
The way the water flows through the spout and through the body are potentially symbolic of the way fluids flow through humans/living things. Many Moche mediums depict sexual themes and themes reflective of physiological human features. The unique design of the Stirrup spout may be representative of human physical features, the way the water flows puts the design in line with the Moche themes.

question: What was the context of the creation of this vesse?
answer:
The moche people famously applied artwork to the sides of these vessels with great skill and attention to detail. This style of vase would have been considered an artisan good, crafted by a specialized worker. The formation of the vessel’s shape would also require the skill of a professional. While many similar models make use of physical sculpting of the ceramic to resemble faces and deities, this particular artifact was detailed using a colored liquid clay known as slip to provide red markings across white/beige ceramic. Different degrees of precision and detail reflect the variety of social contexts in which these vessels were employed.
These vessels are exclusive to the southern extent of the Moche region, including the Chicama, Moche and Virú valleys. These valleys are all imbued with fertile, tillable soil, implying that these artifacts were made exclusively in communities with a strong link to agriculture. These vessels were used primarily to store a maize-based alcoholic beverage, further supporting the connection to farming communities. Additionally, the inclusion of (presumably) a lizard on the sides of the vessel is tied to traditions associated with coastal communities in South Peru. The iguana is at times considered a symbol of the power of the Earth and sea, which requires religious and cultural connections to the coast.

question: Who would have used this type of vessel in Moche society?
answer:
It is assumed that single-spouts stirrup vessels were considered more of an artistic medium rather than a utilitarian object. Fine-line slip painting was used to produce intricate drawings of Moche iconography on the bodies of these vessels. These may be a component associated with moche burial tradition, as people of great wealth and status are accompanied by intricate artworks such as these vessels in their tombs. While these are potentially also used in everyday practices, the intricate nature of the stirrup design requires ideal conditions to remain intact. Burial sites often provide an excellent setting for protection of the original structure, mitigating the extent of restoration required. It is thought that these vessels were largely used for funerary and status purposes, but these environments may skew the prevalence of these vessels to appear to be exclusively owned by the highest social classes. However, the techniques required to produce a vessel as intricate as this artifact suggest that this good was reserved for upper class individuals. 
Additionally, these moche vessels would often resemble faces. Some have been identified as portraits of an individual across multiple stages of life. This has led some research to suggest that, while the shape is often mass-produced using molds, each vessel is unique and reserved for high-society individuals, specifically in ritualistic and funeral capacities. The vessels were likely filled with maize beer and left in tombs with religious and political leaders to accompany them into the afterlife.
